# XML parser that resolves external entities (C#)

`qualor:csharp/xxe` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-611](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/611.html), [CWE-776](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/776.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A02:2025 Security Misconfiguration](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A02_2025-Security_Misconfiguration/), [A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A05_2021-Security_Misconfiguration/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
XML parsers from System.Xml that are set up to read what a document's DTD points at:

- an `XmlReaderSettings` with `DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Parse` and an `XmlUrlResolver` as its `XmlResolver` (in an object initializer, or as statements in the same method);
- an `XmlDocument` given a `new XmlUrlResolver()`;
- an `XmlTextReader` given a `new XmlUrlResolver()`, unless its `DtdProcessing` is set to `Prohibit` or `Ignore` (it parses DTDs by default).

The rule looks at how the parser is configured, whatever the document; it does not need request data. The defaults are safe and are not reported: `XmlReaderSettings` prohibits DTDs, and with no resolver set (the default of `XmlReaderSettings`) external references are not fetched. Test code is skipped.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
An XML document can declare entities that point at files or URLs (XML external entities). A parser that resolves them puts the content of a local file, or the answer of an internal service, into the parsed data, which often ends up in a response or an error message. Entity expansion can also exhaust memory and CPU ("billion laughs"). Setting an `XmlUrlResolver` is what turns the fetching on, so it is the line to avoid.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** DTDs are parsed and an `XmlUrlResolver` fetches what they name.

```csharp
using System.IO;
using System.Xml;

public class InvoiceParser
{
    public XmlReader Open(Stream input)
    {
        var settings = new XmlReaderSettings();
        settings.DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Parse;
        settings.XmlResolver = new XmlUrlResolver();
        return XmlReader.Create(input, settings);
    }
}
```

**Compliant:** the defaults refuse DTDs and resolve nothing.

```csharp
using System.IO;
using System.Xml;

public class InvoiceParser
{
    public XmlReader Open(Stream input)
    {
        var settings = new XmlReaderSettings();
        return XmlReader.Create(input, settings);
    }
}
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Keep the defaults: `DtdProcessing.Prohibit` and no `XmlResolver`. Create readers with `XmlReader.Create` and `XmlReaderSettings`, not `XmlTextReader`.
- If a document must have a DTD, use `DtdProcessing.Parse` without a resolver (or with `XmlResolver.ThrowingResolver`), and set `MaxCharactersFromEntities` to a small limit; use `DtdProcessing.Ignore` to skip the DTD without failing.
- Remove `XmlResolver = new XmlUrlResolver()` from `XmlDocument` and `XmlTextReader` code that reads input you do not control. When a resolver is needed, use one that only serves known local files, or `XmlSecureResolver` limited to a trusted location.
- On .NET Framework before 4.5.2 the default resolver fetches: set `XmlResolver = null` on `XmlDocument`, `XmlTextReader` and `XmlReaderSettings` there.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- System.Xml

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- Only `new XmlUrlResolver()` counts as a resolver. One kept in a variable, returned by a helper or written as a custom `XmlResolver` class is missed.
- For `XmlReaderSettings`, `DtdProcessing.Parse` and the resolver must be set in the same block or the same initializer, as literals; set in different methods they are missed.
- `DtdProcessing.Parse` without a resolver is not reported: external references are not fetched with the defaults of .NET Framework 4.5.2 and later, .NET Core and .NET 5+. Such a parser still expands internal entities without a limit unless `MaxCharactersFromEntities` is set. Before .NET Framework 4.5.2 the default resolver fetched, so a bare `XmlTextReader`, `XmlDocument` or a `Parse` setting was unsafe there; the rule does not know the target framework.
- An `XmlDocument` with an `XmlUrlResolver` is reported even when it is loaded through an `XmlReader` that refuses DTDs.
- Code in a file OpenGrep cannot parse (some C# 11 and 12 syntax: `$$"""` raw strings, `class X : Y;`, some multi-line collection expressions) is not checked.
- Files under `test/`, `tests/`, `*.Tests/`, `*.UnitTests/`, `*.IntegrationTests/`, `*.Test/` and `*.Specs/` and named `*Tests.cs` or `*Test.cs` are skipped.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test file [`rules/csharp/xxe/xxe.cs`](../../../rules/csharp/xxe/xxe.cs) holds every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.

The rule: [`rules/csharp/xxe/xxe.yml`](../../../rules/csharp/xxe/xxe.yml), added in version 2026.10.5.
